messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Vignette:
Linh Tran is a 60-year-old Vietnamese American woman who has been married for thirty-five years and works as a call center agent at a regional insurance company. She came to the clinic in the spring, nearly eighteen months after the death of her daughter, Mỹ Linh, who was thirty-two years old and eight months pregnant when she collapsed without warning at home from an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia. By the time the ambulance arrived, both Mỹ Linh and the baby — a girl who would have been named Cẩm — were gone. Linh had been on the phone with her daughter in the minutes before it happened, listening as the call went silent, hearing nothing and then hearing everything: the thud, a neighbor's voice, the confusion. She had not been there. That fact had settled into her like sediment.

In the weeks that followed, Linh moved through the funeral arrangements in a state of functional numbness. She recalls standing at the cemetery and feeling as though she were watching herself from somewhere above the treeline. She has not returned to that cemetery since, and she has told her husband she never will. When a coworker's mother passed away last winter and the office circulated a sympathy card, Linh signed it quickly and left the room. She cannot explain this to her colleagues, only that something closes in her chest when grief becomes public and visible — a wreath on a door, a black dress in a shop window, the particular quiet of a memorial service. She had come to believe that exposure to these things would pull her under in a way she would not be able to manage.

Her work at the call center has become its own minefield. Linh handles general customer inquiries, and on several occasions she has been connected to callers reporting a newborn on a policy or asking about adding a baby to a family plan. The first time it happened she sat frozen at her desk for several seconds before transferring the call without explanation. Now she has quietly arranged with a supervisor — without disclosing the reason — to have infant-related calls redirected when possible. But this accommodation is informal and unreliable, and on the days it fails her, she finds herself in the break room afterward, hands wrapped around a cup of tea she does not drink, staring at the wall. When she hears a baby crying in a store or in the apartment building where she lives, she describes a sensation of the floor tilting beneath her, followed by a surge of feeling she can only call terrible — fear and something older and heavier that she has no single word for.

The memory of what happened does not come to her as a continuous story. There are moments of excruciating clarity: the exact pitch of the silence on the phone, the grain of the kitchen table she was sitting at, the light through the window. And then there are stretches that are simply gone, as though the tape has been cut. Sometimes a fragment surfaces without warning — the sound of her own voice saying her daughter's name — and then it is gone again before she can hold it. When she notices herself beginning to approach the fuller shape of the memory, something intervenes, and she finds herself thinking about something else entirely, standing at the sink, or suddenly very interested in a task. She has come to understand this as a kind of protection, though she is not sure protection from what, exactly.

Linh has pulled back from the friends she and her daughter shared, the women from their temple community who knew Mỹ Linh as a child. She has not attended temple in fourteen months. Her husband has stopped asking her to come. Most nights she lies awake for one or two hours, her mind moving in tight circles, before sleep finally arrives shallow and unreliable.

What brought her in was a conversation with her husband, who told her gently that he was worried he was losing her too. She had not realized, until he said it, how much smaller her life had become. What she is most afraid of, sitting in the intake chair, is that fully remembering will mean fully losing — that if she lets the memory complete itself, the grief will be permanent and unsurvivable. What she hopes, though she does not quite believe it yet, is that someone might show her otherwise.
